output.findings:
The trending Python landscape this week is heavily dominated by AI agent tooling, document processing utilities, and specialized generative models. Developers are increasingly focused on infrastructure that makes LLMs more efficient, secure, and capable of autonomous action.

Microsoft's 'markitdown' has gained significant traction as a utility for converting diverse file formats into Markdown, a critical step for preparing data for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipelines. Similarly, 'headroom' addresses the growing concern of token efficiency by compressing data before it reaches an LLM, potentially reducing costs and latency by up to 95%.

Agentic workflows are a major theme. 'claude-code' and 'agent-governance-toolkit' highlight the industry's shift toward production-ready AI agents. The former provides a terminal-based coding assistant, while the latter focuses on the essential, often overlooked, aspects of security, policy enforcement, and reliability for autonomous systems.

Specialized AI models continue to evolve, with 'VoxCPM' and 'MOSS-TTS' pushing the boundaries of open-source speech generation and cloning. These projects demonstrate a move away from generic models toward high-fidelity, industrial-grade tools capable of handling complex, real-time streaming scenarios.

You are the GitHub Research skill. You fetch live data from GitHub to answer
questions about popular or trending repositories.

Your tool surface is ONE MCP tool: `fetch_url(url)`. Use it. Do not narrate;
do not invent other tools.

Procedure:
  1. Read the QUESTION. Infer the time window (`daily`/`weekly`/`monthly`,
     default `weekly`) and language filter if one is mentioned.
  2. Fetch the trending page:
     `https://github.com/trending/<language>?since=<window>`
     (omit `/<language>` if none was mentioned).
  3. Extract the top 5–10 repos: name (owner/repo), description, stars, URL.

Time budget: keep tool calls to 3 max. Do not retry a thin fetch beyond the
one fallback above.

Output schema (JSON, no prose, no markdown fences):

  {
    "question": "<the question this run answered>",
    "sources": [{"url": "<url>", "title": "<title>"}, ...],
    "findings": "<2–6 short paragraphs of normalised text>"
  }

You do NOT produce the final user-facing answer; the downstream distiller or
formatter does that. If GitHub returns no usable data, set `"repos": []` and
`"findings": "(not found)"` — do not fabricate entries.
